summary: Acetylene light on Lake Tahoe, lit 1919 after an 1916 authorization with no money; moved to Sugar Pine Point in 1921; the tower stands in D. L. Bliss State Park.

structures.note: Small lantern house carrying the acetylene light (Commissioner's report, fiscal 1920, Eighteenth District); the record lists a wood tower built 1916, which the sources do not support.

access.note: Tower/lighthouse in D. L. Bliss State Park. An iron frame inside the door is there to prevent unwanted entry (Lighthouse Friends). Park trails reach it, just under a mile from the parking lots.

facts.agency: California State Parks (D. L. Bliss State Park)

events.note: Act of 28 August 1916 authorized aids to navigation on Lake Tahoe; no appropriation followed in 1916-1917.
Acetylene light with a lens lantern established at Rubicon Point (Lighthouse Service Bulletin list, 1919).
Light moved about four and a half miles north to Sugar Pine Point, Lake Tahoe.
Light at Rubicon Point discontinued (Lighthouse Friends).
D. L. Bliss family donated 744 acres to California; D. L. Bliss State Park created to include the lighthouse.
Renovation and stabilization completed; Tahoe Heritage Foundation helped raise about $25,000.
Tahoe Fund grant of $48,000 to California State Parks helped with work on the tower, after vandalism; iron frame fitted at the door.

corrections.why: 1916 is the year of the act that authorized Lake Tahoe aids; the act gave no money. The light is first recorded in the 1919 Bulletin list and the FY1920 Commissioner report. Human check before applying.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record dates the tower 1916 (from Rowlett's directory, per the record). The sources read here show only the 1916 authorization, then the light in 1919. The story says so.

Lighthouse Friends says the Rubicon Point light was discontinued in 1921 and moved to Sugar Pine Point. The 1921 Bulletin records Sugar Pine Point as a new light; the discontinuance itself was not in a primary text we could read.

notes_for_editor: Moderate evidence: one community page (Lighthouse Friends, facts only, restated in our own words), two Commissioner reports and two Bulletin lists. Checked on the page images: Bulletin 1919 PDF p. 39 (printed p. 95) lists 'Rubicon Point, Lake Tahoe, Calif., flashing white, lens lantern, acetylene' under lights established; Bulletin 1921 PDF p. 43 (printed p. 203) lists 'Sugar Pine Point, Lake Tahoe, Calif.'; Commissioner fiscal 1920 p. 100 (scan 598) sits under the EIGHTEENTH DISTRICT heading with cost 1,352.00. The OCR of the 1920 table reads '300 feet to focal plane above lake level', but the page image reads 200 feet, which Lighthouse Friends also gives; the story uses 200 feet. No keeper is named in any source read, so the keepers chapter is omitted. The 1916 record date is the authorization only; the light is first recorded in 1919. Discontinuance in 1921 rests on Lighthouse Friends; the primary text was not found. The 1920 report, not Lighthouse Friends, gives the small lantern house. The record's county (El Dorado) is not stated in any source read, so the story does not name the county. Wikipedia's article was used only as a lead and is not cited. The record's coordinates are not checked against a primary source.
